Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

shinytone (development version)

  • Start page: rows without f0 are removed, and the gaps are marked. A new Data screening box in the Start sidebar has token, time and f0 pickers, and screens the chosen f0 variable when a file is uploaded (before an upload it shows its heading and a one-line note). Its Remove N rows without f0 (recommended) box is ticked by default, for pitch-tracker frames and equidistant points alike. The rows go before any tab sees the data; the uploaded file is not changed, and unticking the box brings them back. A new integer column, voiced_run, numbers the stretches with f0 in each token (1 up to the first gap, 2 after it, and so on), so the gaps stay marked once the rows are gone. Other boxes appear only when they have something to do: Also remove runs of 1–2 samples cut off by a gap at a token’s start or end (unticked; not offered when every token has the same number of points, where such a gap flags its token); Read 0 / -1 as no f0 (ticked), for an Hz column such as f0_rapt that zero_hz_to_na() does not pick; and, when every row has f0 but the time steps show gaps, Mark the N gaps in a voiced_run column (ticked), which removes nothing. Without a token variable, the box counts the rows without f0 over the whole file and asks for the token variable only when it needs one. One message on upload sums it up, with the 0 Hz count. The other tabs start on its f0 and token variables. New exported screen_f0_rows() (the counts), drop_rows_without_f0() (the removal), suggest_unvoiced() (values that may mark no f0) and hz_f0_columns(). landmark_prefixes() reserves voiced_run.
  • Start page: a report on the upload. Above the Data Preview, a Your data card gives the tokens, speakers, tones and rows, how the f0 is sampled (pitch-tracker frames, their step and how many tokens have a gap in the middle; N equidistant points per token with the tokens that have fewer or more; or uneven points), and the variables used. A Data screening card, the same for frames and equidistant points, gives the share of rows without f0, says where they are (at a token’s start or end, or inside it) and what the boxes do: how many rows removal takes (“Removed: 16 rows without f0”), or “All good: every row has f0” when there are none to take. A folded Your raw file is not changed note, shown whenever the app’s copy differs from the file, says to download that copy in Normalise or Curate. The card also names short runs cut off at a token’s edge, other Hz columns and the rows where they differ, rows deleted in F0 Correction, token-level columns (speaker, tone, metadata) that change within a token, and a time column whose 0-1 decision would change with the rows removed. A warning that gaps cannot be found from the time steps appears only when it matters: when neither rows without f0 inside the tokens nor a voiced_run column show the gaps, and never for equidistant points. Frames with the same number in every token count as points in both cards.
  • Start page: tokens with an issue are flagged, and can be dropped. A new column, screen_flag, gives each flagged token’s reasons on every row (“” for the other tokens): no f0, or fewer than 3 samples with f0 (either reason stands alone), and, when every token has the same number of points N, no f0 at the first or last point, or points without f0 inside (a gap of any length). In such a file a token is flagged when it has fewer than N points with f0. The column is added when a token is flagged and the drop is unticked, and it replaces a screen_flag column the file already has (left out when no token is flagged now). One box, Drop the N flagged tokens (unticked), leaves them all out; it appears when a token is flagged. A token with no f0 is flagged like the rest, whatever the removal box says, and counts in the box, the message and the report. When every flagged token has no f0 and removal is ticked, the report says that removal takes their rows. The report says what the flagged tokens share (“5 tokens flagged: fewer than 11 points with f0”). For equidistant points it lists them grouped by reason, one line each: points without f0 inside, no f0 at the first or last point, and fewer than 3 points with f0 (tokens with no f0 among them), with at most 5 tokens per line. For frames it names them in brackets. The flags and the drop come before the removal of rows without f0, and the R code repeats them. New exported flag_f0_tokens(). screen_f0_rows() also lists the tokens left with 1 or 2 samples (few_samples, few_tokens) and the tokens missing an end point (edge_missing, edge_tokens, edge_rows).
  • Normalise: Download Normalised Data saves every column of the data it normalised, with the new columns at the end, as the other tabs get it. It used to save only the columns shown in the table, so an f0-only run had no token or time column.
  • Start page: what each tab does comes first. The welcome text is followed by a folded Continuing from the F0 Correction tab? box and then the list of tabs, which now includes Cluster and Curate; What the data look like follows. Both Start pages (F0 Analysis and F0 Processing) list their tabs with one Font Awesome icon each, on a pale circle coloured by the stage of the work (data, prepare, explore, model, summarise), in place of emoji.
  • F0 Processing Start page: a syllable tier for multisyllabic words. Its companion-files note now says that a .TextGrid with a syllable tier is highly recommended for multisyllabic words, so the analysis can line up the syllables across tokens. The note is set off by a soft yellow bar, and Already have f0 extracted with another tool? is a folded guide box.
  • A larger top menu, and what a token is. The top menu (About, F0 Analysis, F0 Processing, Data Collection) is now 17 px, a step larger than the sub-tabs below it. Data Collection > Filename says in one sentence what a token is: one recording of one syllable or word by one speaker, that is one .wav file and the rows of f0 data that share its token ID.
  • About page: an optional export step in workflow 3. In Pitch-tracking correction, a dashed (optional) F0 Extraction (export) step now follows F0 Correction. F0 Correction saves the cleaned CSV directly. For another region (the whole token or a TextGrid interval) or sampling (native frames or equidistant points), export it from F0 Extraction instead, which picks up the corrections made in the session. Workflow 2 no longer shows the Start page as a step, like the others.
  • Pickers say “variable” throughout. The Start page’s pickers (Data screening, contour duration and the metadata pickers) and the F0 Processing tabs’ pickers now say “variable” (e.g. f0 variable, Token ID variable, Time variable, Token / filename variable), as the F0 Analysis tabs already did, and so does the text that names them. Text about a column the app adds, such as voiced_run, or a column of a metadata CSV still says column.
  • Gaps read from the time steps. Once rows without f0 are removed, a gap shows only as a longer time step. A step more than 1.5 times the token’s usual step is a gap: a one-frame gap doubles the step, so a 2x rule would miss it. The usual step is the token’s median step or, in a token with fewer than 5 steps, the file’s common step when that is smaller. Steps are read only on a regular grid, where one step and two are clearly apart and the times are written finely enough, so points timed at each glottal pulse are not read. A token with two samples with f0 at the same time is set aside, and the other tokens are still read. Times written to the step itself, such as 10 ms frames written to 2 decimals, are read in whole units: a step of 0.02 s or more is a gap. This needs at least 99% of the steps to be exactly one unit. So such a file is not read from its time steps when more than 1 step in 100 is a gap, or when its frames are not 10 ms apart (12.5 ms, say); when that matters, the Start page says how many decimals to save the times with (3 for 10 ms frames, 4 for 12.5 ms). A token where at least 2 steps, and more than 1 in 8, are exactly 2 units is set aside. The same rule serves the Start page, the jump check, contour_duration(), trim_to_voiced() and flag_f0_gaps().
  • 0-1 time axes run from the first f0 to the last. A 0-1 axis is there to compare contour shapes, and stretches without f0 carry no tone. normalise_time_token() now runs each token from its first f0 (0) to its last f0 (1), and normalise_time_landmarks() runs each segment of a tier, such as each syllable, from its first f0 to its last; the TextGrid boundaries only say which rows belong to which syllable. Before, they ran from the token’s first row to its last and from each interval’s start boundary to its end, so a voiceless onset put the first f0 at, say, 0.2. <tier>_tseq puts the syllables in sequence: syllable 1’s f0 fills 0 to 1, syllable 2’s fills 1 to 2, and a stretch without f0 at the boundary takes no room. token_t01 is the whole-word option: it keeps the gap between the syllables and their duration ratio. Rows before the first f0 or after the last are NA, not 0 or 1, and so are segments with f0 at fewer than two times, rows in empty-label intervals and rows outside the tier. So removing rows without f0 changes none of these columns. A lone sample cut off by a gap at a token’s edge still sets its 0 or 1; the Start page’s short-run box removes such samples. Both functions gain f0 (default "f0"), and normalise_time_landmarks() gains token (default "token"), as segments are taken within each token. In a column in Hz, 0 is no f0. A column with negative markers such as -1 is not read as Hz, so its -1 and 0 values count as f0: set them to NA first, or tick the Start page’s box that reads them as no f0. A missing column is now an error rather than a silent no-op, <tier>_tseq is no longer added without a <tier>_i column, and data with an f0_corrected column get a message to pass f0 = "f0_corrected". Columns saved by earlier versions keep their old values and are still used as they are by their names: make them again in Normalise.
  • <tier>_tbound: syllables in sequence, with the gap kept. normalise_time_landmarks() adds a third column next to <tier>_t01 and <tier>_tseq. The TextGrid boundaries between a word’s syllables are at 1, 2, …, so they line up across tokens, as on <tier>_tseq. A stretch without f0 at a boundary keeps its length, as on token_t01. The word’s first f0 is at 0 and its last f0 at n, the number of syllables, so stretches without f0 at the word’s edges take no room. A syllable with no f0 at all at the word’s start or end gets NA, and the word then starts at 1 (or ends at n - 1). One GAMM smooth over <tier>_tbound can follow an f0 jump across the gap; on <tier>_tseq both sides of the jump sit at the same time. Removing rows without f0 or reordering the rows changes nothing. The column needs <tier>_i, and it needs time and the boundaries on the same clock, as F0 Extraction writes them: a token whose time lies outside its own intervals gets NA, with a message. fit_gamm() keeps it on its own 0 to n scale, like <tier>_tseq; the other fits and compute_mean_contour() rescale it per token from the first f0 to the last. landmark_prefixes() keeps <tier>_tbound free for the tier.
  • The fits rescale time from the first f0 to the last too. resolve_time_norm() gains f0, and fit_gca(), fit_gamm(), fit_polynomial() and compute_mean_contour() pass their f0 column, so rows without f0 at a token’s edges no longer move the time axis. Fits, mean contours, Chao numerals and Timing are now the same with or without these rows, and a fit on the time column matches a fit on token_t01. On a test set of 1,853 tokens with rows without f0 at every edge, the Chao numerals with the rows kept were 32, 212, 323, 54, 315/415 and 214; they are now 32, 212, 32, 45/55, 31 and 213, as with the rows removed. These functions and cluster_features() also read 0 in an Hz column as no f0, as the axes do, rather than as a pitch of 0. Without f0, resolve_time_norm() keeps its first-row-to-last-row rescale.
  • Syllables in sequence: two rows at each boundary. On <tier>_tseq, one syllable’s last f0 and the next one’s first f0 share a whole number, often with an f0 jump between them. compute_mean_contour() and cluster_features() never average the two: at the boundary and just after it they use the next syllable’s f0, and just before it the earlier one’s. They tell the rows apart by <tier>_t01 or <tier>_i, so the row order does not matter. Other rows of a token at one time, such as two recordings that share a token name, are averaged, with a message that names the tokens. One GAMM smooth over <tier>_tseq cannot follow a jump at a boundary; the fit_gamm() help suggests <tier>_tbound or token_t01 for the whole word, or one token per syllable on <tier>_t01.
  • Landmark axes in auto mode. time_already_normalised() gains name. A column named <tier>_t01, token_t01 or time_prop whose values all lie in [0, 1] counts as already normalised by its name, so removing rows cannot switch the fits to a rescale. resolve_time_norm() and the app pass the name. A <tier>_tseq is still judged by its values. On the Model, GCA and GAMM tabs, a <tier>_t01 with one part per token (a word, rhyme or vowel tier) counts as a whole-token axis, like token_t01: it gets the “already on 0-1” note, not the multisyllabic warning.
  • Normalise: three ways to put a word on one axis. Time normalisation reads which rows have f0 from the f0 (Hz) variable the tab normalises, offers the token picker for tiers too, and no longer offers a 0-1 axis as the time variable. A tier adds <tier>_t01, <tier>_tseq and <tier>_tbound, and the message after the run names all three. The guide says what the new column is and why tokens need it, and names the tier columns by their endings (<syllable_tier>_t01, _tseq, _tbound; token_t01 keeps its name whatever the token variable is called). Its pictures show one token in time on top, with a ruler for each axis, then, in a row, the three choices for a word, each with a card under it saying when to use it: In sequence (_tseq: the boundaries line up), In sequence, gap kept (_tbound: the boundaries line up and the gap is kept) and Whole word (token_t01: the gap and the syllables’ relative durations are kept, so the boundary moves from token to token). The layout follows the guide’s width: three in a row, then each picture beside its card, then each above it (on a phone); on narrow screens Token A switches to a narrower drawing. The Whole word card says to pick a word tier with only the target word labelled when a token holds more than the word, such as a carrier phrase. The first tip names every tab that takes the new column. The table shows the time, token and <tier>_i columns next to the new axes. When time and the boundaries are not on the same clock, a second message says why <tier>_tbound is NA.
  • Visualise: in sequence, gap kept. Align by TextGrid tier (renamed from Align time by landmark) offers three layouts, named after the chosen tier: In sequence (<tier>_tseq), In sequence, gap kept (<tier>_tbound) and Overlaid (<tier>_t01) (In sequence was Side by side). In sequence, gap kept is new and plots <tier>_tbound. Both layouts in sequence draw dashed lines at the boundaries and now name each part at its middle (“syllable 1”, not “1”). Show R code makes the same axis. A tier without <tier>_i offers Overlaid only; a tier with it offers all three again, with the layout picked before.
  • GAMM: a note for <tier>_tbound. On a <tier>_tbound with several syllables per token, the GAMM tab says that the fit keeps its 0 to n scale and that the gap is kept, so one smooth can follow an f0 jump across it. The note on <tier>_tseq, where one smooth cannot follow such a jump, now suggests <tier>_tbound or token_t01 for the whole word, and so do the red warning on a <tier>_t01 and the multisyllabic guide. Model and GCA give a <tier>_tbound the same nudge to GAMM as a <tier>_tseq. With several syllables per token, the GAMM tab now starts on <tier>_tbound, where one smooth can follow an f0 jump at the boundary; Model and GCA still start on <tier>_tseq. When <tier>_tbound is empty for some tokens (time and the boundaries on different clocks), GAMM starts on <tier>_tseq too.
  • Jump check: the same flags with or without rows without f0. flag_pitch_jumps(), and so inspect_f0() and the Inspect tab, now set aside rows without f0 (NA, 0 or a negative marker) and rows with no time, check the rest in time order and map the flags back. Rows set aside are never flagged, so the flags are the same with or without them and in any row order. Each sample is compared with the next sample that has f0, with the rate scaled by the real time step. On a regular grid, a jump across a gap gets ” across a N ms gap” in its note, where N is the step minus the usual step, so a one-frame gap in 10 ms frames reads as 10 ms. Across a gap, the flag goes on the shorter side when it is a run of at most 5 samples, since a short fragment cut off by a gap is the likelier error; otherwise on the side farther from the token median, as before. Negative values and NA times no longer stop the check. inspect_f0() gives a token with no f0 the note “no f0” and no flags, counts the level check’s speaker x tone groups over tokens with f0, and keeps a voiced_run column.
  • contour_duration(), trim_to_voiced() and flag_f0_gaps() find gaps without the rows. A run of f0 now also ends at a time step longer than 1.5 times the usual step (on a regular grid) and where a voiced_run column changes, so these functions give the same result with or without the rows without f0. Before, removing them could join a stray frame in the silence to the contour: 6 of the 1,853 test tokens gained 20 to 60 ms of duration. With set, contour_duration() finds the gaps over the whole token, then counts each segment’s own rows. For a token with no rows without f0, flag_f0_gaps() keeps the file’s own n_missing and has_gap, which may record rows removed earlier, instead of resetting them, and sets has_gap where the time steps or voiced_run show a gap. All three gain run (default "voiced_run").
  • GCA: the polynomial basis is built on the rows the model fits. fit_gca() resolves the time axis on all rows, then keeps the rows the model fits (a finite time, f0 and tone, and the speaker and item the model uses) and builds poly() on those. Before, rows without f0 inside tokens shifted the basis and so the coefficients, and a landmark axis with NA time stopped with “missing values are not allowed in ‘poly’”. On data with no rows without f0, the fit is unchanged. Too few rows for the degree now give a clear error. The fit records time_coverage, each tone’s first and last fitted time, and predict_gca() carries it. The GCA tab’s Show R code keeps the same rows before poly().
  • GAMM: the AR1 correction starts afresh at every token. With use_ar1 = TRUE, fit_gamm() put each token’s AR.start on its first row by time. When that row had no f0, as at the edges of a whole-file track, bam() left the row out and the marker with it, so the AR1 correction ran on from one token into the next. The marker now sits on each token’s first row that the model fits. On the test set, all 1,853 markers had been lost, which moved the curves by up to 1.2 LZ. On a <tier>_tseq, time_range and n_segments now come from the fitted rows, so predict_gamm() spans the part of the axis the model was fitted to (0 to n on a <tier>_tseq from normalise_time_landmarks()), not rows without f0 at the edges; its tones and reference speaker and item come from the fitted rows too. Rows at the same time keep their input order, so give each token’s rows in time order. diagnose_gamm() whitens the residuals along the model’s own AR starts. The fit records time_coverage, which predict_gamm() carries. The GAMM tab’s Show R code keeps the fitted rows, puts the marker on the first of them, estimates rho within tokens, and runs with a speaker-by-tone random smooth, where its prediction step used to fail.
  • contour_to_chao() checks the time axis. Time must run from 0 at the onset to 1 at the offset. Time outside [0, 1], such as milliseconds, point numbers or a GAMM across several segments of a <tier>_tseq, is now an error; such input used to give numerals read at the wrong points. A contour that starts after 0.25 or ends before 0.75 gives a warning. A factor time column is read by its labels. Rows with no tone, time or f0 no longer set the f0 range, and a tone with f0 at fewer than two time points is left out, with a warning. New columns t_first and t_last give where each tone’s contour starts and stops. When it misses 0 or 1, its onset or offset is read from the nearest measured point, held flat, and move, progress and timing use that value; progress is still read at 0.5 on the time axis. Summarise marks such a tone with a dagger (†) and a note, and does the same for GCA and GAMM predictions whose fitted rows stop short of 0 or 1.
  • Summarise fixes. An error in the mean contours or the Chao conversion, such as a text column chosen as Time, now shows a message and clears the old table and plot, instead of closing the app; warnings from the conversion show as messages too. The guide opens with “One syllable per token”: for a multisyllabic word, make each syllable its own token on <syllable_tier>_t01 (numbered by <syllable_tier>_i), labelled by the word’s tone pattern and its place. When the tab declines Chao numerals for a GAMM fit across several segments, the message now says to model each syllable as its own token on <syllable_tier>_t01. The Timing guide says the middle of the tone is halfway between its first and last f0. The curated route takes its token and f0 variables from the Start page, and the menus keep the user’s picks when the data change. The Praat script page says that its CSV covers whole files, silence included, and that Data screening on the Start page removes the rows without f0 by default.
  • Model, GCA, GAMM and Summarise: a notice only when it matters. An amber notice at the top of these tabs appears when a time column used as it is (already on 0-1) leaves some token’s f0 short of 0 or 1: time_prop over a region whose end points have no f0, or a 0-1 column made by an older version. It counts those tokens (or syllables, on a <tier>_t01), says whether removing rows changes it, and how to fix it. It never appears on the real time column, which the fits rescale from the first f0 to the last.
  • Token labels from the rows with f0. fit_polynomial(), cluster_features(), compute_mean_contour(), flag_outliers() and flag_level_outliers() take a token’s speaker and tone as the most frequent non-empty value on its rows with f0 (a tie goes to the value that comes first in time), not from its first row. A label column read from a TextGrid tier, such as a tone tier with "" in the silences, can change within a token, so the first row used to depend on the row order and on the rows without f0. fit_polynomial()’s checks for tokens with too few samples now count only rows with f0 and time.
  • Results from old rows are cleared. A new upload already cleared every result computed from the previous file. Now so does a change on the Start page that changes the rows the tabs read: a box under Data screening, the screened variables, Exclude discarded tokens, metadata or duration columns. Normalised, inspected, clustered and curated + normalised data, GCA and GAMM predictions and each tab’s shown results are cleared, with a message that names them and the change. Curate’s relabels and exclusions are kept, as they are keyed by token. A change that leaves the rows as they were clears nothing.
  • Variable defaults follow the Start page. The token and f0 menus of the F0 Analysis tabs default to the Start page’s token and f0 variables, so an F0 Correction file is analysed on f0_corrected, not the tracked f0. Normalised columns still come first where a tab prefers them, and time defaults are as before. The Start page’s token picker never falls back to another column (a file of points with no token column was grouped by its point number), and its time picker leaves out *_t01, *_tseq and *_tbound. A menu keeps the user’s own pick. When a tab’s f0 variable is not the screened one and still has rows without f0, a note under the menu says so.
  • Show R code repeats the Start page. The R code of Visualise, Model, GCA, GAMM and Summarise now rebuilds the rows the app used, in the order the Start page runs its steps: the read and zero_hz_to_na(), the exclusion of tokens discarded in F0 Correction (missing before), the metadata join (as code when the file and key are known, otherwise as a comment), the contour_duration() lines, and drop_rows_without_f0() with min_run and unvoiced when used. Comments give the counts, and a commented screen_f0_rows() line reproduces the report. The code starts with stopifnot(utils::packageVersion("shinytone") >= ...) for the version the app runs on, since these functions need it. The Model, GCA and GAMM scripts rescale time from each token’s first f0 to its last, as the app does.
  • Inspect tab. Shares of flagged samples are counted over the samples with f0, so they are the same whether or not the Start page removed rows. The time unit is set from the data (a median step within tokens below 1 means seconds) and shown under the buttons, e.g. “Frame step 10 ms”, with a warning when the chosen unit does not fit. Before, millisecond data left at “s” silently turned off the rate test. A failed run shows a message instead of closing the app. The guide describes the comparison with the next sample that has f0, the gap note and where the flag goes across a gap.
  • Plot lines break at gaps. Curate’s plots and Visualise’s Align by TextGrid tier plot draw one line per voiced run when the data have voiced_run, so a line no longer bridges a gap where the Start page removed rows without f0. Curate’s selection, click and hover still work by token, and Visualise’s Show R code groups the lines the same way. The aligned plot now calls normalise_time_landmarks(), so each part runs from its first f0 to its last, as in <tier>_t01 and <tier>_tseq, and its Show R code prints that call. Which rows have f0 comes from the Start page’s f0 variable, even when Y is another variable. Alignment now needs a token variable.
  • F0 Extraction: Drop rows without f0 marks the gaps. The export option now uses drop_rows_without_f0(), so the file carries a voiced_run column. With equidistant points or a TextGrid interval region, only the dropped rows mark gaps. The help says that Curate and Visualise break the line at each gap either way, and that other plotting tools join the line across the removed rows unless they group by voiced_run. A re-uploaded file’s voiced_run is not carried over: the export makes it again.
  • Changed arguments. New arguments come last, so positional calls still work. contour_duration(), trim_to_voiced() and flag_f0_gaps() gain run = "voiced_run". flag_outliers() and flag_level_outliers() gain time = NULL, used only to break a tie between labels. normalise_time_landmarks() gains f0 = "f0" and token = "token", and normalise_time_token() gains f0 = "f0"; a missing column is now an error. resolve_time_norm() gains f0 = NULL, and time_already_normalised() gains name = NULL. contour_to_chao() returns t_first and t_last, and stops on time outside [0, 1]. fit_gca() stops with “Too few rows to fit” when fewer than degree + 1 distinct time points remain. fit_gca() and fit_gamm() return time_coverage, which predict_gca() and predict_gamm() carry as an attribute. New exports: screen_f0_rows() (its run reads the gaps an earlier removal marked), drop_rows_without_f0(), suggest_unvoiced() and hz_f0_columns().
  • CSVs and TextGrids in UTF-16 and other encodings. Praat saves tables and TextGrids as UTF-16 whenever any text is not plain ASCII, such as Chinese token names or IPA labels. A UTF-16 CSV used to close the app, and a UTF-16 TextGrid was silently ignored (no tiers, no TextGrid strip, empty landmark columns). Every upload now reads UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32, with or without a byte-order mark. A file in an older code page is read as Chinese (GBK, Big5) or Western European text, with a note to check it. A file that cannot be read, such as an Excel workbook or a binary TextGrid, gives a message saying why, and the app keeps running. Praat’s --undefined-- reads as NA. The new read_csv_utf8() and read_textgrid() read files the same way in R.
  • Landmark columns keep non-ASCII tier names. Tiers named 声调 and 音节 now give 声调_start and 音节_start, not tier_start and tier_1_start, and F0 Extraction no longer leaves the second one out of the download. A clash (two tiers with the same name once cleaned, or a tier named time) gets _2, _3 in a fixed order, and the notification says so. ASCII tier names keep their old columns unless two differ only in case. New landmark_prefixes(); attach_landmarks() gains all_tiers.
  • 0 Hz f0 is read as missing. Pitch trackers write 0 Hz for unvoiced frames. In a CSV uploaded in the Start tab these zeros counted as pitch values: they pulled contours, fits and plots towards 0 and gave -Inf in semitones, which could close the app in the Model tab. The Start tab now reads 0 Hz in f0 columns as NA and says how many rows changed; other columns, including normalised ones, are left alone. normalise_f0() treats f0 of 0 or below as NA for every method, and the Model tab shows an error instead of closing. Show R code reads the file the same way. New zero_hz_to_na().
  • Chinese text in static plots. Visualise, GCA, GAMM and Summarise plots and their downloads now show Chinese tone, speaker and tier names. When labels contain Chinese characters, the plot uses a Chinese font installed on the machine, so 阴平 and 阳平 no longer both appear as 平. If none is found, the app says so once. A font file placed in inst/app/cjk-font/ is used first. Interactive plots are unaffected.
  • Chinese tone names in their usual order. Legends, facets, tables and menus sorted 阴平 阳平 上声 去声 by code point, as 上声 去声 阳平 阴平. Traditional tone names, in simplified or traditional characters, now sort 平 上 去 入 with 阴 before 阳, so GCA and GAMM fits take 阴平 as the reference tone. A factor keeps its own levels, and other labels keep their order. New sort_tones().
  • GCA and GAMM plots: readable axis numbers. In the app, the axis numbers of the GCA and GAMM prediction plots were tiny or missing, and the text was not in the app font. Both plots now use the same theme as the Visualise plot, on screen and in the downloaded PNG.
  • Small fixes. The Start-tab preview says when a file could not be read and shows the real row count for files under 10 rows. Faceted Visualise plots have more room between panels.
  • Chao numerals: timing of rises and falls. The numerals give pitch levels, not when a tone moves, so an early and a late rise between the same levels get the same digits. contour_to_chao() now also returns move (the change from onset to offset), progress (the share of it done at 0.5 on the time axis, the middle of the tone) and timing: "early" above 0.75, "late" below 0.25 and "mid" in between. They are given for a rise or fall of at least half a unit with no sampled turning point, and are NA otherwise. The numerals themselves are unchanged. In the app, the results table has a Timing column, in red when the value at 0.5 is within the fuzzy margin of a cut-off, and the CSV and the R code carry it. On the sample data, tones 3 and 6 are late and tone 5 is mid.
  • Non-ASCII tone labels. compute_mean_contour() no longer stops with “Character encoding must be UTF-8, Latin-1 or bytes” when tone labels are non-ASCII text read by read.csv(), as the app reads uploads (for example Chinese tone names). This affected the Summarise and GCA tabs.
  • Summarise guide: shorter. The Chao numeral guide is shorter, and its data source list marks GCA / GAMM predictions and normalised f0 as recommended with a thumbs-up. The sidebar help, the parameters line and the note on red values are shorter too.
  • Summarise: new Chao figure. Both panels label every sampled point (onset, any dip or peak, offset) with its digit in the tone’s colour, moved apart with a short leader line when they would overlap. The reference-line panel marks lines 1 to 5 with digit chips at the right; the interval panel shows each band’s digit as a large watermark. The pink zones mark digit boundaries ± the fuzzy boundary threshold, with a legend entry. Colours are colour-blind safe, the two panels line up exactly, and the downloaded PNG uses Open Sans like the app. The plot code lives in inst/app/ui/summarise_plot.R.
  • Summarise: turning-point threshold. A new “Turning-point threshold” input (default 0.5 Chao units, as before) sets how far a dip or peak must go beyond both endpoints to add a middle digit. The results table has a “Dip / peak” column with each tone’s dip or peak, in red when within the fuzzy margin of the threshold, and a note gives the numerals the other side of it would produce. On the sample data, tone 6 dips by 0.43, so it is 23 at the default and 213 at 0.4. The CSV and the R code carry the threshold. contour_to_chao() now returns dip and peak columns and a threshold attribute, and checks threshold.
  • Chao numerals: a middle digit only where it shows the turn. Each scale keeps the middle digit only if it differs from both endpoint digits. A middle digit that repeats an endpoint digit merges into it, as the turn is too shallow to show at five levels: 23, not 223 (which reads as a late rise), and 22, not 222. The two scales round differently, so a tone can get two digits on one and three on the other; contour_to_chao() gains n_digits_int for the interval numeral (n_digits is the reference-line one). When a contour both dips and peaks beyond its endpoints, the larger turn is now sampled (the dip used to be checked first), so a lower threshold never removes a digit. On the sample data, tone 2’s interval numeral changes from 112 to 12. In the app, the left-out value is shown in grey brackets in the Scaled column, a note lists those tones, the figure marks the point with a hollow dot, and the near-threshold flag now only marks tones whose numerals would change. Clearing the fuzzy boundary threshold box no longer stops the conversion, and the R code panel handles flat contours (zero range) as the app does.
  • Normalise again after Curate. The Normalise tab can now read the Curated data (new “Data source” menu, shown once you have curated). This recomputes each speaker’s mean (and SD) on the kept tokens and the new tone labels, and creates a new Curated + normalised data set. Visualise, Model, GCA, GAMM and Summarise list it; Model, GCA and GAMM switch to it after each such run, and Summarise picks it unless model predictions exist. The curated data itself is not changed. Normalised columns left over from the first run are dropped, so only the column this run made remains (e.g. f0_st, not a stale f0_lz). The set is cleared if the curated tokens or labels change afterwards (or the curation is reset), with a note to normalise again; re-normalising the uploaded data does not clear it. Downstream tone and speaker menus default to the variables used in Curate and Normalise (e.g. cluster). Normalise’s variable menus now have their own input IDs; they shared tone_var and speaker_var with Visualise, so one tab’s choice could silently change the other’s. Once curated data exists, the Normalise tab starts on it; Curate’s route boxes add a step 4, “Normalise again”, and Model, GCA and GAMM show a reminder while “Curated data” is chosen. Path 5 of the About page workflow (and the paper’s copy, paper/figures/workflow_overview) now reads Curate, Normalise, Model, Summarise: the normalisation used for analysis comes after curation, and normalising in path 2 only helps Curate’s display. Figure boxes drop “(optional)”; the dashed border and legend say it.
  • A new upload starts afresh. Uploading a file (including “Try with our sample data”) now clears everything computed from the previous file: normalised, inspected, clustered, curated and curated + normalised data, GCA/GAMM predictions, and each tab’s shown results (Normalise table, polynomial, GCA and GAMM fits, clustering, Chao conversion), with a note saying so (and a line under the Start tab’s sample-data button says it up front). Before, the previous file’s normalised data stayed in the menus, and Model, GCA and GAMM selected it by default, so trying the sample data and then uploading your own could model the sample. Curate’s relabels and exclusions are reset too; they used to carry over and, on a re-uploaded curated CSV, overwrote <tone>_original.
  • Summarise: normalise first. The data source menu lists Normalised f0 (and Curated + normalised f0) first. The Hz routes are now labelled “Uploaded f0 (converted to LZ here)” and “Curated f0 (converted to LZ here)”, with a tip to normalise first so Chao numerals and models share one scale. Picking a z-score column shows a note that z-scores are linear in Hz; on the sample data, Hz or z-score against semitones or LZ changed 4 of 6 tones’ numerals. The curated route now uses the tone variable chosen in Curate (e.g. cluster).
  • cluster_features() resamples to 21 points by default (was 20), one every 5% of the stretch from each contour’s first to its last f0 value. This is the same default as the app’s Cluster tab, resample_f0_equal() and compute_mean_contour().
  • compute_mean_contour() resamples tokens instead of binning their samples. It used to assign each sample to the nearest of 50 time bins and average the samples in each bin, so with unequal numbers of f0 points per token each bin averaged a different subset of tokens, and a token with more than 50 points counted more than once in some bins. Every token is now interpolated at the same time points, by default 21 (one every 5%, as in cluster_features()), and counts at most once at each: nothing is extrapolated beyond a token’s first and last f0 value. Measured points that fall on the grid, such as 11 or 21 equally spaced points per token, keep their values when each token’s first and last points have f0, or on time_prop. n_bins is deprecated in favour of n_points. The mean contours of the Chao tab and the GCA tab’s observed overlay use the new method.
  • Summarise: the robust Chao method is removed. Its range, one SD beyond the mean peak of the highest tone and the mean valley of the lowest, suited single tokens but not the averaged contours the numerals are read from: it squeezed them towards the middle digits, so 5 and 1 were rarely reached. It also moved more with pitch-tracking errors than the range of the averaged contours used by the other two methods, and Zhu (1999), the source cited for it, had tested this range and found it worse than the plain extremes. contour_to_chao() no longer returns the robust and rob_continuous columns or the robust_stats attribute; raw_data, raw_token, raw_f0 and raw_tone are deprecated and ignored, with a warning. The Chao tab, its CSV download, plot and generated R code show the reference-line and interval methods.
  • Summarise: raw f0 is converted to LZ by speaker before Chao conversion. The Raw f0 and Curated f0 sources averaged Hz over all speakers, so higher and lower voices were mixed in the mean contours. Each speaker’s f0 is now converted to LZ (log z-score, Zhu 1999) before the mean contours are taken. The Raw f0 source has a speaker selector (or none, for one speaker), and curated data find the speaker column by name. The summary says how many speakers were normalised and gives the ranges in LZ, the generated R code includes the step, and a raw source whose f0 has negative values is refused as already normalised. The README, the vignette and the contour_to_chao() examples now normalise before converting.
  • Summarise: reference-line values near a rounding edge are flagged. For the reference-line method, the red highlighting in the Chao table and the grey zones in its plot marked values near the reference lines 1 to 5, where the digit is clear, instead of near the rounding edges at 1.5, 2.5, 3.5 and 4.5, where it is not. Both now mark the rounding edges, using the fuzzy boundary threshold chosen in the sidebar. The note under the table states that threshold instead of a fixed ±0.1, and the guide says where each method’s digit boundaries lie.
  • Summarise: generated R code finds turning points. The R code shown under the Chao table now detects turning points as the app does, so a dipping or peaking tone gets its three-digit numeral there too; it used to sample only the onset and offset, so every numeral had two digits. The guide also states that the conversion is linear in the units of the input, so the input sets the pitch scale: semitones and LZ give a log-frequency scale, Hz and z-scores a linear one.
  • Summarise: IPA tone letters. The Chao numeral table has a “Letters” column for each method (35 as ˧˥, 214 as ˨˩˦), and the CSV download has matching columns. The app bundles a 6 KB tone-letter subset of Charis SIL (renamed under its Open Font License, inst/app/www/fonts/OFL.txt), so a run of letters joins into one contour line for every visitor. The new chao_to_letters() converts numerals to letters in the package, one letter per digit, so a level tone keeps both (55 as ˥˥).
  • About: “Community & reach”. A new section at the bottom of the About page shows the project’s GitHub stars, as a line built from the date of each star, and the views and downloads of the Zenodo archive. A daily GitHub Action (.github/workflows/usage-stats.yaml) collects these public figures into usage.json on the usage-data branch, and the app’s server reads that file (cached for 6 hours), so the page never waits on it, new figures appear without redeploying, and visitors’ browsers do not contact GitHub or Zenodo. Zenodo reports only running totals, so its line starts on the first day of recording.
  • Normalise: log z-score (LZ) option. normalise_f0(method = "lz"), and “By-speaker log Z-score (LZ)” in the Normalise tab, add an f0_lz column: the z-score of log10 f0, (log10 f0 - mean) / sd with the speaker’s mean and SD of log10 f0 (Zhu 1999); any other base gives the same LZ. It works on ratios like semitones and also evens out speakers’ pitch ranges. It is the usual “z-score” in studies of tone in languages of China: 37 of the 136 studies in Xu & Zhang (2024) used it, against 4 that used a plain z-score. speaker_mean is then the geometric mean in Hz, and f0 of 0 or below counts as missing. The default stays "semitone". In the Normalise and Inspect tabs, the “f0 (Hz)” selector now prefers an Hz column over normalised ones. The About page no longer lists ERB, which normalise_f0() never offered.
  • Normalise: “equally weighted by tone” now also weights the z-score SD, and the SD correction is a choice. With mean_method = "weighted" (the default) every tone already counted once in the speaker’s centre, but the z-scores still divided by an SD pooled over all frames, so a tone with many tokens shaped the scale: two speakers with identical tones but 50/50 versus 90/10 token counts got LZ tone means of ±0.99 versus ±1.65. The SD is now weighted the same way (as stats::cov.wt()), for both "zscore" and "lz". mean_method = "simple" keeps the classic Rose
    1. z-score and Zhu (1999) LZ, and the two agree exactly when every tone has the same number of f0 values. A new sd_correction argument (default TRUE: Bessel’s correction, the n - 1 sample SD; FALSE divides by n), shown in the Normalise tab as a “Bessel’s correction for the SD (n − 1)” checkbox for the z-scores, makes that step visible. This changes "zscore" output with the default weighted mean whenever tones have unequal numbers of f0 values (unequal token counts, unvoiced frames, or tokens of different lengths): on sample_f0, where some speakers have a token or two more or fewer of some tones, each speaker’s SD moves by −0.9% to +2.2%. Semitones are unchanged, and "zscore" now returns the same class as its input (it used to return a tibble).
  • F0 Correction tab: TextGrid tier names are no longer cut off. The plot’s left margin was fixed at 60 px, so a name longer than about seven characters lost its start (“phoneme” showed as “honeme”). The margin now fits the longest tier name across the uploaded TextGrids, the same for every token, up to 150 px; a longer name is shortened with “…” and shows in full on hover. The names come from the new tg_tier_names(), which scans TextGrid text for tier headers (long or short format, UTF-8 or UTF-16) instead of parsing each file, so it is quick enough for a whole corpus. The selection band on the plot is also a lighter grey.
  • F0 Correction tab: play part of a token, as in Praat. Select a stretch on the plot and it is shaded light grey across the waveform, f0 and TextGrid, staying shaded through redraws, zooming and panning. One selection serves both listening and editing: a box or lasso on the f0 dots selects the dots inside it, while a drag on the waveform or a click on a TextGrid interval (Shift-click, or drag along the tier, to span several) selects every dot in that stretch, so the dots the edits act on always lie inside the grey band. A click on one dot selects just that frame; a double-click or Q clears the selection. (Before, a drag on the waveform, or a box with no dots in it, left the earlier dots selected, so Delete could hit frames outside the stretch in view; and clicking the same dot again after selecting elsewhere was ignored.) Plotly’s dashed box now shows only while dragging. Then press Tab (or P), or Selection on the new play bar above the plot, to hear just that part; with no stretch selected it plays the visible part, which is Praat’s rule. Tab again stops, and a red playhead follows the playback. The play bar also has Visible and Stop, and reads out the selection’s start, end and duration. The audio player above still plays the whole file. Playback goes through the Web Audio API, so the slice is sample-accurate rather than limited by the ~250 ms granularity of an <audio> element’s time updates, and each slice fades in and out over 5 ms (and fades out when stopped part-way), so cutting the sound mid-wave does not click. The synthesised contour has its own Selection button, mapped onto its own clock, and S plays the same stretch from it (the corrected contour once you have edited), so the recording and the f0 track can be compared over the same stretch.
  • F0 Correction tab: the synthesised contour now plays in real time. sonify_f0() synthesises only the stretch from the first to the last voiced frame, but the duration it was given was the span of every frame, silence included, so the voiced contour played slowed down to fill the whole file (1.7x on a token with 0.37 s of edge silence). It now runs at the voiced stretch’s own duration, so it lines up with the recording.
  • Model: GAMM tab keeps a <tier>_tseq axis on its own scale. For multisyllabic words the guide routes you to fit on syllable_tseq (syllable 1’s f0 fills 0–1, syllable 2’s fills 1–2), but fit_gamm() rescaled each token’s time to 0–1 like any other column. That moved the syllable boundaries away from whole numbers, and the plot showed a 0–1 axis. fit_gamm() now recognises a _tseq column and uses it as-is (time_normalised = "sequential" declares any such axis). predict_gamm() predicts across the range of the rows it fits, and the fit records time_axis, time_range and n_segments. The GAMM plot keeps the 0-to-n axis, marks each segment boundary with a dashed line, and labels the segments. The tab explains the axis when _tseq is chosen, and Show R code reproduces all of it. Summarise now declines Chao numerals for such a fit, since they describe one syllable on a 0–1 axis.
  • Axis titles: f₀ (st) for semitones. The GAMM plot labelled its y axis with the raw column name (Predicted f0_st); it now uses the same title as the other tabs (Predicted f₀ (st)). Semitone axes read f₀ (st) rather than f₀ (semitone) throughout: Visualise, Curate, Cluster, GCA and GAMM.
  • F0 Analysis Start tab: add a contour duration column. A new Add contour duration block under Attach metadata adds how long each f0 contour lasts: the time from the first to the last frame with f0, per token (token_f0_dur) or per landmark segment such as each syllable (syllable_f0_dur), repeated on every row of the unit. Unvoiced frames at the edges do not count, and unvoiced frames inside the contour do not shorten it. The ends are anchored on two voiced frames in a row with no gap between them, the rule the Whole token export region uses, so a lone stray frame in the silence cannot stretch the duration; a whole token’s value then equals the voiced_s that F0 Extraction reports. The value is the same whether or not the Start page removes the rows without f0, and when it reads 0 or -1 as no f0 in the same column, so does the duration. The column reaches every F0 Analysis tab. Also scriptable as contour_duration() (min_run = 1 for the literal first-to-last frame), which counts negative values as measured, so it works on semitone or z-score columns too.
  • F0 Extraction tab: Drop rows without f0 export option. The Whole token region already leaves out leading and trailing silence but keeps unvoiced gaps inside the contour as f0 = NA rows. A new checkbox (off by default) drops those rows too, for tools that expect measured values only, and marks the gaps in voiced_run (see above). It runs last, so resampling still sees the gaps and has_gap / n_missing still flag the tokens. With equidistant points, a token with a gap then keeps fewer than N points, each still labelled by point and time_prop.
  • F0 Extraction tab: 0 Hz in an uploaded f0 CSV reads as unvoiced. The wrassp and .Pitch paths already turned 0 Hz into NA, but a CSV’s zeros passed through as values and could reach the export inside the region.
  • F0 Processing: edit history survives the F0 Data Export round trip. The export writes corrected values into f0 but recorded nothing about which frames were corrected. Re-uploading it therefore loaded the corrected values as the tracker’s originals, and the next all_correctedf0.csv read edited = FALSE everywhere. When corrections exist, the export now also writes f0_original (the tracker’s value) and edited, and re-uploading either file restores the edits. This works whichever f0 variable the picker is set to: choosing f0_corrected from all_correctedf0.csv used to lose the history the same way. Re-uploading an older export without these columns now shows a note explaining that its corrections cannot be told apart. The export also stops copying correction columns from a re-uploaded file: a token restored in a later session kept a stale token_dropped = TRUE, so F0 Analysis silently excluded it.
  • F0 Correction tab: downloads carry landmark and metadata columns. all_correctedf0.csv and <token>_f0.csv held only the f0 frames plus f0_corrected / edited / token_dropped, so the metadata (uploaded, or derived from filenames) and TextGrid landmark columns set up in F0 Extraction were missing after correction. Both downloads now add them the same way the F0 Data Export does. Re-uploading all_correctedf0.csv to resume keeps these columns, and attaching the same metadata again does not duplicate them: a metadata column the data already holds with the same values is skipped. This also drops the redundant token.meta column that filename-derived metadata used to add.
  • F0 Extraction tab: landmark tiers ticked after extraction reach the export. Landmark columns were attached only when Run extraction was clicked, and the Landmarks from TextGrid picker sits below that button, so ticking syllable afterwards (or in Upload existing f0 CSV mode) left the download without syllable_start / syllable_end / syllable_i. The Normalise tab lists a tier only when those columns exist, so multisyllabic data had no tier to build <tier>_tseq from. The export now attaches any ticked tier the data lacks. An amber note also warns when Equidistant points drops the landmark columns (their boundaries change within a multisyllabic token), and the Normalise tab explains why no tier is listed.
  • F0 Correction tab: two fixes from classroom use. Deleting an outlying frame could leave its “ghost” marker (the original value) drawn off-screen: the f0 panel’s y-range was framed on the corrected values only, and the y-axis is fixed, so there was no way to scroll the original back into view. The range now also anchors on the original values of edited frames. And the Delete button sometimes appeared to do nothing: a click after a box/lasso selection silently kept the stale box (plotly never clears that input on a plain click), so the edit hit the old (often already deleted) frames. The selection now follows whichever of click or box-select happened last, and switching tokens clears it.
  • F0 Correction tab: a note column in the edit log. A Note (optional) box in the sidebar. Whatever it holds is saved with the next edit or discard as the note column of the edit log (table, CSV download, and log re-upload alike), then cleared so it cannot leak onto later, unrelated actions. For recording why: a reason to discard a token, or why frames were removed.
  • F0 Extraction tab: export notes restyled as a banner. The data-quality notes under the export summary (short voiced span, unvoiced gaps, …) were easy to miss as small grey text at the bottom of the sidebar; they are now an amber message box in the same idiom as the Correction tab’s banners.
  • Praat script: version guard for the newer pitch methods. The filtered ac / filtered cc / raw ac / raw cc methods exist only since Praat 6.4 (November 2023); on an older Praat the batch died mid-run with a cryptic “Command not available for current selection” error. The script now checks praatVersion up front and exits with the running version and the fix (update Praat, or pick ac / cc / shs).
  • F0 Extraction tab: F0 Data Export (region + sampling). A new block decides what the downloaded dataset contains, without touching the data in the app: F0 Correction keeps working on the extraction exactly as it arrived, so changing these settings can never disturb frame edits. Region is what the measurement covers: Whole token runs from a token’s first to its last voiced frame, so leading and trailing silence (which carries no f0) is excluded, and an edge needs two consecutive voiced frames so a lone voiced frame stranded in silence cannot stretch it; or a TextGrid interval. Sampling is how densely: every native frame time, or N equidistant points across the region, which is time normalisation applied at the sampling stage and adds point (1…N) and time_prop (0–1). An export preview shows the first rows of the file the Download button will write, metadata join included. New exported functions: resample_f0_equal(), trim_to_voiced(), flag_f0_gaps().
  • Resampling follows Praat’s own rule. resample_f0_equal() ports Sampled_getValueAtX(), which is what Pitch: Get value at time... runs, so a contour resampled here matches one a Praat script gets querying the same times. Of the two frames bracketing a point, the nearer is near and the other far: both voiced blends them, far unvoiced keeps near’s measured value, near unvoiced gives NA. The method argument offers Praat’s two choices, "linear" (default) and "nearest". Unvoiced stretches are respected only when the input marks them as NA (or 0 Hz) rows; sparse input such as a .PitchTier has no such rows, so a silent stretch there is a plain gap between anchors and is interpolated across, exactly as Praat does.
  • F0 Extraction tab: subset f0 by TextGrid interval. Export only the f0 falling inside chosen intervals: vowels found automatically, the rhyme (first vowel to the end of the token; monosyllables only), or labels you type. New exported ipa_vowel_label() and filter_interval_rows(). ipa_vowel_label() handles length marks, stress marks, tone digits and Chao letters, combining diacritics, precomposed pinyin tone marks (ā ǎ ū ǔ …) in either Unicode normalisation, di- and triphthongs including j/w/ɥ offglide spellings (aj, ɔw) as well as ai and au, and syllabic nasals (m̩, n̩, ŋ̩) as vowel-equivalent nuclei.
  • Two checks that make silent problems visible. flag_f0_gaps() adds n_missing and has_gap, marking tokens whose voicing was interrupted mid-region, measured on the native frames before resampling, since resampling can fill a short dropout from the nearer frame. (On data whose rows without f0 were removed, it reads the gaps from the time steps or voiced_run and keeps the file’s own values; see above.) And the per-token summary reports voiced_s with voiced_prop (voiced_s / duration_s), shading and naming tokens voiced across a far shorter span than the rest of the corpus: with equidistant sampling their percentage positions are squeezed into whatever was tracked, so they are not comparable with the other tokens.
  • Modelling: an already-normalised time column is used as-is. fit_gca(), fit_gamm(), fit_polynomial() and compute_mean_contour() gained time_normalised ("auto", "no", "yes"). Under the default "auto", a column that is already proportional (token_t01 from normalise_time_token(), or time_prop from equal-point extraction) is detected by the new time_already_normalised() and used as-is, rather than rescaled a second time, which stretched any token not spanning the full unit interval. The Model, GCA and GAMM tabs say when this applies and their Show R code output reflects whichever branch ran; fit_gca() and fit_gamm() record time_prenormalised in the returned object, fit_polynomial() as an attribute. Columns named <tier>_t01, token_t01 or time_prop are recognised by their name (see above). For other columns, detection is deliberately conservative and has two documented limits: a set in which every token is a partial span cannot be distinguished from ordinary variable-duration time and is rescaled as before (pass "yes"), and raw seconds in which every token lasts just under one second is detected as proportional (pass "no").
  • 0 Hz counts as unvoiced in the new f0 helpers, matching inspect_f0() and the extraction paths, so trackers that code unvoiced frames as 0 Hz are handled rather than having silence blended into speech.
  • The multisyllabic warning no longer fires on token_t01. On the Model, GCA and GAMM tabs it is now raised only for a landmark tier’s <tier>_t01 with more than one part per token, which resets at every segment boundary, and not for the whole-token proportional axis, which is a perfectly good time variable.
  • F0 Correction tab: whole-token discard. A new “Whole token” edit group adds Discard token / Restore token for tokens that are beyond repair: instead of fixing frames, the whole token is marked as dropped. Non-destructive, since the f0 values are kept and both downloads gain a token_dropped column (TRUE for discarded tokens) to filter on downstream. Discarded tokens show a ✗ in the token picker and a banner above the plot, appear in the edit log (Undo restores, as does the Restore button), survive the save/re-upload resume cycle via the new column, and a “Kept + discarded / Only kept / Only discarded” filter joins the edit-status drawer. Keyboard: X discards the current token, or restores it if already discarded, so a review pass can run entirely on , . and X. The sidebar progress line and every discard notification report the running share of the corpus discarded, e.g. “Discarded: 812 of 8000 (10.2%)”.
  • F0 Correction tab: bulk discard of flagged tokens. Once an Inspect-tab CSV is loaded in the filter drawer, a Discard all flagged tokens button marks the entire flagged set as discarded in one click. The confirmation dialog reports how many tokens that is and what share of the corpus they represent. This is the fast route for large corpora: discard the flagged set, then optionally review it (“Only discarded”) and Restore any worth repairing. A Restore all button next to the discard toggle un-discards every discarded token, bulk and manual alike, and removes their edit-log rows.
  • F0 Correction tab: discard-share breakdown by speaker and tone. The corpus-wide discarded share can look harmless while the discards pile up in one speaker or tone; in the worst case a whole speaker × tone cell is emptied and vanishes from the retained data. When the filter drawer’s speaker / tone columns are picked (auto-guessed from the uploaded Inspect CSV), the bulk-discard confirmation dialog shows what the discard set would look like per speaker × tone cell with marginals (“After this discard”), and a Breakdown button next to the discard toggle reopens the same table for the current state. Cells are discarded/total (%), tinted red when a group would be fully discarded and amber at half or more, with tokens absent from the CSV grouped as “(no metadata)”. With only one of the two columns picked the table reduces to that margin; with neither, the dialog shows the total plus a hint to pick them.
  • GCA and GAMM guides: pointer to model structures the UI does not cover. Both guide boxes now close with a Beyond the built-in options note. The checkboxes and dropdowns cover the structures most often used for tone contours, but lme4 and mgcv support many more: by-speaker tone slopes (1 + (ot1 + ot2) * tone | speaker) or uncorrelated terms via || for GCA; tensor-product interactions such as te(time_norm, duration), or smooths varying by a further factor, for GAMMs. The note directs users to Show R code, which already emits a runnable script reproducing the current fit, as the starting point for editing the model formula.
  • Model: Polynomials tab’s Show R code now reproduces the coefficient scatter. The tab’s generated script used to stop at the coefficient table, leaving the coefficient-space scatter as the one part of the tab with no reproducible counterpart outside the app. The snippet now ends with a plotting section that rebuilds the scatter (one point per token, coloured by tone) using the axes currently selected in the tab (falling back to the plot’s own defaults) and axis labels carrying the phonetic gloss (c1 slope, c2 curvature, …). With no Z axis it emits a static ggplot2 scatter; with a Z axis selected it emits the matching 3-D plotly::plot_ly(type = "scatter3d") call instead, mirroring what the tab shows.
  • F0 Correction tab: filter by flag type. When the uploaded Inspect CSV carries flag_notes, a Keep flag types checkbox group lists the artefact classes present (extreme value, level, octave jump, jump by rate of change, carryover, low intensity). Unticking a type hides tokens that carry none of the ticked ones and narrows Discard all flagged tokens to the same subset, so a corpus can be worked one artefact class at a time (e.g. discard the octave jumps, review the level outliers by hand). It combines with the discard-status filter, so the discarded set can be reviewed one flag type at a time.
  • F0 Extraction: Praat is the default f0 source when pitch files are uploaded. Uploading .Pitch / .PitchTier files alongside the audio now selects “Use uploaded .Pitch / .PitchTier (Praat)” automatically and says so, instead of leaving the radio on wrassp and silently extracting without Praat’s per-frame candidate lists. It fires once per session, so a later manual choice is never overridden.
  • F0 Correction: Praat candidates promoted to an edit group. Picking a candidate writes to the contour, pushes undo history and logs an edit row, so the block now sits with the other edit groups (after Manual entry) rather than below the Display checkboxes. When no .Pitch data is loaded it shows a short hint explaining how to enable the option, so the feature is discoverable from a .wav-only session. The candidate list now spells out that s is Praat’s strength and that the tick marks the frame’s current value, and the empty state mentions that the grey numbered dots on the plot can be clicked directly. The Display checkbox “Top-3 Praat candidates on f0 plot” is greyed out and unticked when the data carries no candidates, rather than sitting ticked over an overlay that cannot appear, and its caption explains that dot 1 is the value Praat chose (2 and 3 are its next alternatives), that not every frame has three candidates, and that the unvoiced candidate is not numbered.
  • F0 Correction: plot mark legend. A “Marks:” strip above the plot names every non-obvious mark: f0 value, selected frame, Praat candidates (dot 1 being Praat’s own pick, click to apply), the two sample-level flags in parallel wording (“jump or carryover”, red fill; “low intensity”, a bare amber ring that can sit on any fill colour), edited frames, and the outlined circle showing a frame’s value before the edit. Entries appear only when the corresponding data exists. When an Inspect CSV is loaded, a tinted status box under the key summarises the current token: light coral (dot-red border) whenever the token is flagged, with the frame counts and flag classes, or, for a token-level flag with no flagged frames (extreme value / level), a pointer to look at the whole contour; amber when the only signal is the advisory low-intensity ring; green with an explicit “nothing flagged by Inspect”. Flagged states add the reminder “Flags are leads, not errors: verify by eye and ear before editing” on its own line.
  • F0 Correction: low-intensity frames marked on the plot. Frames the Inspect tab flagged as low intensity now carry an amber marker ring (reading flag_low_intensity when present, else the flag_notes text). Kept deliberately distinct from the red fill: red means a probable tracking error, the amber ring only means the f0 estimate there is less reliable. The ring co-exists with the red/blue fills, hover text says “low intensity (f0 here is less reliable)”, the legend names it “flagged by low intensity”, and the “Keep flag types” filter’s Low intensity class now has a visible counterpart on the plot.
  • F0 Correction: re-extraction no longer strands earlier edits. After re-extracting on a different engine or frame grid (e.g. Praat first, then wrassp), edits made on the old grid were kept keyed by token name: the tab silently served the stale contour, and because the row counts no longer matched, ghost markers, the amber halo, and the “N frames edited” banner all vanished for that token while edits still appeared to apply. Frame edits that no longer align with the data are now cleared on re-extraction (with a notification); whole-token discards, which are name-keyed and still meaningful, survive.
  • F0 Correction: the idle reminder dismisses itself. The “Still working?” note that appears after ten idle minutes used to stay until closed by hand; the first interaction after it fires now takes it down (it returns after the next ten idle minutes).
  • Curate tab: “Flagged” now covers every Inspect check. The amber highlight, the “Flagged” quick-select, and the flagged-count chip now use flagged_token (any check: extreme max/min, unusual level, frame-level jumps) instead of only the “level too high / low” notes, so the exclude machinery can also serve as a whole-token disposal path for artefact-flagged tokens.
  • Start tab: discarded tokens honoured. Uploading a CSV that carries the F0 Correction tab’s token_dropped column (e.g. all_correctedf0.csv) now pops a notification reporting how many tokens are marked discarded and excludes those rows (and the flag column) from the working dataset by default; a sidebar checkbox (“Exclude discarded tokens”) restores them. The uploaded file itself is never modified. Previously the discarded tokens flowed silently into every downstream tab (Normalise, Inspect, Visualise, the models, Summarise).
  • Bulk-discard guidance. An illustrated “Big corpus, small flagged set? Bulk discard and review” guide joins the F0 Correction tab, walking through flagging in Inspect, discarding the set, and the optional review pass. When a corpus is large but lightly flagged (at least 1000 tokens with at most 15% flagged; thresholds in offer_bulk_triage()), the Inspect summary and the F0 Correction flagged-CSV loader suggest that route proactively.
  • flag_outliers() (the speaker-level extreme-value screen) is now one-sided: a token is flagged too_high only when its per-token maximum is unusually high (z_max > z_threshold), and too_low only when its minimum is unusually low (z_min < -z_threshold), replacing the previous two-sided abs(z) > z_threshold. Gross tracking errors are directional (octave-doubling or a spurious spike inflates the maximum; octave-halving, a subharmonic, or creak deflates the minimum), and because the screen pools all of a speaker’s tones the opposite tails hold legitimate low/high tones rather than errors. This makes the flag_too_high / flag_too_low columns, and the “max too high” / “min too low” notes from inspect_f0(), directionally correct; before, a token with an unusually high floor could be mislabelled “too low”. The set of flagged tokens is essentially unchanged on clean data (the rarer truncated-max / floored-min cases are left to flag_level_outliers() and flag_pitch_jumps()).
  • inspect_f0() now accepts tone = NULL, which skips the tone-relative token-level check (flag_level_outliers()) and omits the tone column from the output, so it can run before tone categories are known (e.g. the clustering / tone-discovery workflow). The speaker-level extreme-value and sample-level jump checks still run, and the default remains tone = "tone", so existing calls are unchanged.
  • Inspect tab: optional tone. The tone selector now offers (none), which runs the two tone-free screens (speaker-level extreme-value and sample-level jumps) without a tone column, for the pre-tone-discovery workflow. Backed by inspect_f0(tone = NULL).
  • GAMM tab: on-demand diagnostics. The “Run model diagnostics” button is shown in the sidebar from the start (disabled until a model is fitted), and diagnostics run when it is clicked rather than automatically after every fit, so fitting stays fast.
  • GAMM diagnostics (new). diagnose_gamm() and a “Model diagnostics” section on the GAMM tab: after fitting, one click reports the basis-dimension check (k’, edf, k-index, p-value, flagging under-resourced time smooths), the four gam.check() residual panels (Q–Q, residuals vs fitted, histogram, observed vs fitted), the residual ACF, and the concurvity table, with a text download of all diagnostics. The ACF is computed per token (in the spirit of itsadug::acf_resid()) and AR1-whitened when the fit used an AR1 correction, so it shows whether the correction actually worked.
  • GCA fit-over-data overlay (new). The GCA tab now optionally overlays the observed per-tone mean contour (semi-transparent points, computed with compute_mean_contour()) on the fitted polynomial curves, so you can judge how well the chosen degree tracks the data (the standard GCA model-adequacy check, Mirman 2014). Toggle it with the “Overlay observed per-tone means” checkbox; turn it off for a cleaner plot on busy data. The overlay is included in the downloaded plot.
  • The GAMM tab’s AR1 correction is now on by default: densely-sampled f0 frames are strongly autocorrelated, so smooth p-values are anticonservative without it. fit_gamm() (whose use_ar1 argument still defaults to FALSE) now estimates rho from the lag-1 autocorrelation within tokens rather than across the flat concatenation, so token boundaries no longer bias the estimate.
  • run_app() now checks GitHub once per launch for a newer shinytone release (2-second timeout, silent when offline) and, when one exists, prints the update command in the console and shows a one-time notification in the app. Disable with options(shinytone.check_updates = FALSE).

shinytone 1.0.0

First stable release. The Shiny app covers the citation-tone workflow end to end (collect, extract, inspect, correct, curate, normalise, cluster, visualise, model, Chao numerals), and the analytical functions behind each step are exported and documented. Highlights since the 0.1.x line:

  • Contour clustering (new). An unsupervised “tone discovery” workflow that groups tokens by f0-contour shape when the number of tone categories is unknown (Kaland 2023). New functions: cluster_f0() (k-means, hierarchical Ward, or Gaussian-mixture clustering), cluster_features() (represent each contour as resampled points, Legendre / DCT coefficients, or its derivative), choose_k_f0() (suggest the number of groups via silhouette, gap statistic, and a minimum-description-length cost), cluster_mdl(), and cluster_agreement() (adjusted Rand index against provisional labels). Surfaced through the new Cluster tab.
  • Contour sonification (new). sonify_f0() renders an f0 contour as an audible waveform: a pure tone, a complex tone (12 harmonics, band-limited below Nyquist), or a source-filter synthesised vowel (a / i / u), with the pitch gliding along the contour. An optional intensity argument shapes the loudness envelope from per-frame dB. The Cluster tab’s “Listen to the contours” panel plays each candidate cluster’s mean contour back, so prototypical tones can be heard, not only seen (faithful Hz when an Hz column is present, or shape-only on a chosen base pitch).
  • Hear your corrections (new). The F0 Correction tab sonifies the contour you are editing as an Extracted vs Corrected A/B pair, played at the token’s own duration with loudness following the measured intensity, so you can hear whether an edit fixed the pitch track.
  • Intensity made visible (new). In F0 Correction, the f0 dots are sized by per-frame intensity (louder = bigger), with a size legend and per-frame dB on hover.
  • Curate (new). apply_relabels() re-labels tone-category variants (splits or mergers, colloquial vs. literary readings, sandhi) or excludes mis-elicited tokens without overwriting the original labels, surfaced through the new Curate tab.
  • TextGrid landmarks (new). When Praat .TextGrid files are supplied, the F0 Extraction step can attach per-frame landmark columns from a chosen interval tier: <tier>, <tier>_start, <tier>_end, and <tier>_i (segment index). New functions: tg_interval_tiers(), assign_tier_landmarks(), and attach_landmarks(). The Visualise tab can then align contours by these landmarks, including syllable by syllable for multisyllabic words.
  • Landmark time normalisation (new). normalise_time_landmarks() rescales time within each segment, adding a within-segment 0–1 axis (<tier>_t01) and a sequential, word-level axis (<tier>_tseq). A normalise_time_token() companion rescales the whole token to 0–1 (no landmarks needed, for monosyllabic data). Surfaced through a new “Time Normalisation” section on the Normalise tab. The model tabs default the Time variable to <tier>_tseq when present and steer multisyllabic analyses toward GAMM.
  • F0 Processing. The Start preview now flags audio files too short to yield an f0 frame and skips them during extraction. flag_low_intensity() (the intensity-based inspection check) is now exported and documented.
  • Visualise palette (new). The tone colour scale is a 12-colour set matched to the app theme, replacing the pale default so every tone reads clearly on a white background.
  • Faster start-up (new). A one-time “loading analysis tools” toast appears the instant the page connects while the heavy analysis packages load in the background, so the landing page paints immediately.
  • Praat extraction script (new). The bundled script writes readable text .Pitch files, samples per-frame intensity into the CSV, and resolves the chosen CSV output path correctly on Windows.

shinytone 0.1.2

  • New flag_level_outliers(): a third inspection layer that compares each token’s overall level (its median f0, in semitones) against other tokens of the same speaker and same tone using a robust modified z-score (median/MAD; Iglewicz & Hoaglin 1993, cutoff 3.5). It flags smoothly shifted contours — e.g. a low-tone token mis-tracked up into the mid-tone band — that the pooled max/min check and the sample-level jump check both miss. Surfaced through inspect_f0() (new level_threshold and min_tokens arguments, level too high / level too low notes) and the Inspect tab.
  • The "norm" (normalised-time) option was removed from time_unit in flag_pitch_jumps(), inspect_f0(), and the Inspect tab: the rate-of- change thresholds are physiological (ST per 10 ms) and have no meaning once real time is discarded. Inspection runs on real-time data (s / ms).
  • Inspect-tab guide rewritten around three complementary layers, and the “Pitch-tracking quality check” workflow now marks Normalise as optional (inspection runs on raw f0).

shinytone 0.1.1

  • flag_pitch_jumps() (and therefore inspect_f0() and the Inspect tab): when a sample-to-sample jump is detected, the flag is now placed on whichever side of the jump is farther from the token’s median f0, rather than always on the landing sample. This correctly identifies the artefact whether it sits at the start or the end of a sequence (e.g. an octave doubling on the first frame of a token, which the previous landing-only logic mis-flagged).
  • Carryover now walks both forward AND backward from each flagged sample, so artefact runs that begin or end the token are extended in both directions.
  • Inspect-tab guide text and flag_pitch_jumps()’s function docs describe the new median-aware logic as an adaptation of the rate-of-change + carryover approach in Steffman & Cole (2022).

shinytone 0.1.0

  • First public release as an R package, alongside the existing online Shiny app at https://chenzixu.shinyapps.io/shinytone/.
  • Package skin only at this stage: the Shiny app continues to run unchanged. Standalone analytical functions (normalise_f0(), fit_gca(), fit_gamm(), contour_to_chao(), …) will be extracted in subsequent releases.
